I like the snub nosed revolvers just fine.

There is a secret you should know; they have a reputation for inaccuracy, but that's mostly a lie. Their mechanical accuracy is no less than that of a comparable, longer-barreled revolver, and when we are talking about modern guns in good condition, that level of accuracy is surprisingly high.

What is true is that the sight radius is shorter, which means you need to put the front sight exactly in alignment with the rear, or you will miss. If a longer barreled gun had three times the sight radius, the sighting error could be three times greater to produce the same result. In practical terms, this means that an obvious sight misalignment on the larger gun would be barely noticeable in the smaller one. You can defeat this by simply being aware of it.

A second issue is that they kick more, so if you are prone to flinch, it will tend to make it worse. One of the great things about revolvers is that you can load a live round or two, fill the holes with empties, and watch your flinch disappear. When you never know when the gun will fire, it makes the flinch visible, and makes it easy to address. Revolvers also lend themselves wonderfully to dry fire, and dry fire builds muscle memory, and muscle memory is the secret sauce of good shooting.

People who are overweight or normal weight are absolutely harmed by restricting calories or not eating to the degree that it would become an eating disorder. From vitamin deficiencies to stress on your organs, etc. Not all calorie restriction is alike, and there's a healthy kind (eating fewer calories than you expend while still meeting your nutritional needs, aka what fat people need to do) and an unhealthy kind (starving yourself or eating 400 calories a day of food devoid of nutrients, aka what no one needs to do)

You don't prescribe antibiotics for a cold because a cold is virus. I'm not really sure how that relates. I think a more apt comparison would be that there are different stages of the same types of cancer depending on the severity and behavior of the cancer. Like if you have breast cancer, it's all breast cancer, but stage 1 and stage 4 are vastly different stages of the disease with different treatments, different prognoses, etc. Stage 4 is much worse and much more immediately deadly, but if you catch it in Stage 1, it's still cancer, but it's much more treatable and the outlook is better. It's the same with eating disorders; even if someone is not yet down to the point where they have a BMI of 17, they may be on their way there, with no one recognizing the signs because people think all weight loss is 'good' if you aren't 'too skinny.' And, similarly, if the disease is caught before it progresses to a critical stage, treatment is more successful and you are less likely to suffer a lifetime of lasting effects.

Clinicians often diagnose and treat people for having 'subclinical anorexia' or 'subthreshold anorexia' when they are showing all of the symptoms of anorexia but are missing some of the clinical criteria. EDNOS is a less than helpful diagnosis because it can mean subclinical anorexia, bulimia, binge eating disorder, or eating disorders that don't fit the criteria for ANY of those.
